client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. My team is already short-staffed, and then out of nowhere they assigned me this massive project with a deadline that honestly feels impossible to meet. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day the work still has to get done, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — an understaffed team, an overwhelming project, and a deadline that feels out of reach — and that's genuinely a lot to hold all at once. I also hear a little bit of hesitation about whether being here can actually help, and I want to honor that skepticism while also gently saying that sometimes just having a space to untangle the pressure can shift how we approach it. What feels like the most suffocating part of this situation for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, the most suffocating part is just feeling like I'm the only one who actually sees how bad things are at work. My manager keeps acting like everything is fine, like we can just "push through," but I'm the one staying until 9 or 10 at night trying to hold everything together. And then I go home exhausted and I can't even sleep because my brain won't stop running through all the things that could go wrong.
therapist: The exhaustion and isolation you're describing — being the only one who seems to see the reality of the situation while your manager keeps minimizing it — sounds incredibly draining, and it makes complete sense that your mind stays "on" even when your body desperately needs rest. That cycle of late nights, unheard concerns, and sleepless worry can start to feel like a trap with no exit. When you're lying awake running through everything that could go wrong, what kinds of thoughts tend to show up most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It's mostly like... worst-case scenarios playing out in my head, you know? Like I'll imagine making a mistake on a project and my manager throwing me under the bus in front of everyone, or I'll think about how if things keep going this way I might just get pushed out entirely. And then there's this underlying guilt, like maybe I'm not working hard enough or I'm somehow making the situation worse by not being more... I don't know, agreeable or something.
therapist: Those worst-case scenarios — being publicly blamed, pushed out, not being "agreeable enough" — sound like they're working overtime at night, and it's really worth noticing that underneath all of that is a lot of self-blame that seems to be piling on top of an already exhausting situation. In CBT, we'd call those kinds of spiraling "what-ifs" a form of catastrophizing, and the guilt piece is particularly worth exploring — because from everything you've described, it sounds like you're working incredibly hard. I'm curious: if a close friend came to you and described working until 10pm every night while short-staffed and then blamed themselves for not being agreeable enough, what would you say to them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, if a friend told me that, I'd probably tell them they were being way too hard on themselves and that no one could do more than their best in that situation. But it feels different when it's me — like, I know all the ways I've fallen short, all the moments where I could have handled something better or said something differently. It's hard to apply that same compassion to myself because I feel like I actually know the full story, and the full story isn't as clean as I'd make it sound for a friend.
therapist: What you just said is actually a really profound insight — that you'd offer a friend grace because you *don't* know their full story, but you withhold it from yourself precisely *because* you do. But I want to gently challenge that: knowing every moment you *could* have done something differently isn't the same as those moments actually making you responsible for an understaffed, overburdened situation that existed before you. What if the "full story" you know so well is actually being filtered through an exhausted, overwhelmed mind that's primed right now to find evidence against you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard because I was there, I know exactly what I did and didn't do that night. Like, I can replay specific moments where I chose to chart first instead of checking on Mr. Henderson again, and that feels pretty concrete, not just some filtered perception. I guess I just don't know how to separate "I made a mistake" from "I am the mistake," if that makes any sense.
therapist: That distinction you just named — "I made a mistake" versus "I am the mistake" — is one of the most important separations we can make, and the fact that you can articulate it means part of you already senses there's a difference worth finding. What you're describing sounds like it carries a lot of weight, maybe even more than just the work stress we've been talking about — like this moment with Mr. Henderson has become a kind of proof your mind keeps returning to. Can you tell me a little more about what happened that night?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I mean... it was a night shift, and I was covering for two other nurses who'd called in sick, so the floor was already chaos. Mr. Henderson was in room 4, and I knew he'd been showing some signs that worried me, but I got pulled away to handle an emergency with another patient, and by the time I got back to check on him, he'd deteriorated significantly. The charge nurse said I'd done everything by protocol, but I keep thinking — I knew something felt off, and I didn't push harder, I didn't flag it loudly enough, and now I can't stop wondering if that gap of time made a difference.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with this — what you're carrying is so much heavier than a work stress story, and it makes complete sense that it's following you home and keeping you awake. You were one nurse covering three people's worth of care, you responded to an emergency, you followed protocol, and your charge nurse confirmed that — and yet your mind has put you on trial anyway, replaying that gap of time as if you were the one who failed him. I want to ask gently: do you think there's any version of that night where you could have done everything "right enough" that your mind would actually let you off the hook, or does it keep moving the goalposts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. Because when I really sit with it... no, I don't think there is a version where my brain lets me off the hook. It just keeps finding something else — like, okay, maybe I couldn't have been in two places at once, but why didn't I check on him five minutes earlier, or why didn't I push harder to get more staff that night.
therapist: What you just recognized is really significant — that there's no finish line your mind is actually running toward, just an endless relay of new accusations, which tells us this isn't really about finding the truth of that night anymore, it's become a pattern of self-punishment. That kind of relentless internal prosecution, especially after something as painful as what happened with Mr. Henderson, can sometimes be a sign of something deeper that deserves real care and support beyond just reframing thoughts. I want to ask — have you ever had a chance to talk to anyone specifically about that night, or has this been something you've mostly been carrying alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've mostly been carrying it alone, yeah. I told one friend about it right after it happened, but she kind of brushed it off and said "these things happen in workplaces" and I never brought it up again because I felt like I was being dramatic. So in a way, that made it worse, like even the one person I trusted to understand just... didn't, and I think part of me decided it wasn't worth talking about after that.
therapist: What your friend said wasn't dramatic at all — what you experienced was significant, and the fact that the one person you reached out to minimized it didn't mean your pain wasn't real, it just meant she didn't have the capacity to hold it with you. And then you did what so many of us do after we feel unseen: you tucked it away and decided the burden was yours alone to carry, which has made it so much heavier over time. You brought it here today, though — and I want you to know that what happened with Mr. Henderson, and everything you've been carrying since, is absolutely worth talking about.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, I really do, but part of me is still waiting for the other shoe to drop, like maybe you'll eventually think I'm making too big a deal out of something that happened years ago. It's just... I've gotten so used to people either brushing it off or looking at me like I'm broken, so I don't fully know how to just sit here and have someone take it seriously. I guess I'm a little scared of what happens if I actually let myself believe that it mattered.
therapist: The fear you're naming — that letting yourself be seen and taken seriously might somehow lead to more hurt — makes complete sense given how many times you've reached out and been left holding it alone. What strikes me is that you're here, still talking, still letting the words come even while bracing for disappointment, and that takes a quiet kind of courage. I'm not going anywhere, and I want you to know that what happened with Mr. Henderson mattering to you doesn't make you broken — it makes you someone who cares deeply, and that's exactly the kind of person worth taking seriously.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this other part that keeps whispering that you're just saying that because it's your job. Like, it's easy to take someone seriously for an hour when you're being paid to do it — that's not the same as someone choosing to stick around in real life. And honestly, the Mr. Henderson thing still stings because he was supposed to be different, a teacher who actually saw potential in me, and then he just... moved on like I was forgettable.
therapist: The words are coming quickly but there's something quieter underneath them — and I notice you just wove two very different Mr. Hendersons into the same sentence, the patient and a teacher, and I don't want to rush past that. It sounds like being forgotten, or feeling forgettable, is a wound that runs much deeper than any single person — and the fear that I'm just "doing my job" might be connected to that same ache of wondering whether anyone ever chooses to stay simply because *you* are worth staying for. Can you tell me a little more about that teacher?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
